title: Designing From Production Experience
html:
Every design review eventually reaches a question that the architecture diagram cannot settle. At Baodium’s European launch review, it was the first question asked. If the European write path failed at 14:05, which region could accept the next payment at 14:06?

The diagram showed two regions, replication between them, and a payment provider. It left open which region had write authority for a European account, whether the replica contained the last acknowledged authorization, or whether the provider would recognize a retry sent from the other region. Until those facts were established, letting either region retry a payment could create a duplicate or conflicting charge, the Chapter 3 problem on a continental scale.

The review brought together decisions we have examined individually. Adding application instances would affect database connection limits. Failing over to another region could send payment retries from a place that lacked the original operation records. The team also had no European production traffic to validate its capacity assumptions. The launch therefore needed a rule for write authority, a recovery plan for unresolved payments, and gates that could detect when the estimates were wrong. Similar decisions arise when a SaaS platform opens another region or changes a provider that performs critical operations.

Initial Two-Region Deployment

The proposal on the first review table placed application services and a customer database in each region. Both regions could reach the payment provider, and asynchronous replication copied database changes between them. The infrastructure seemed redundant, yet the drawing contained no rule for which region could create an authoritative order after a network partition. Figure Figure records that first proposal as the review found it.

The proposal assumed that another region could take over after a failure. But if the first region acknowledged an order before replication reached the second, part of the payment history could be missing. If both regions accepted writes during a network partition, they could record conflicting outcomes for the same account. The review therefore began by defining what a confirmed purchase meant and which region was permitted to record it.

European Launch Requirements

Before anyone discussed capacity, the team had to agree on what the first release included and what it promised. The European deployment included regional application services, Catalog read infrastructure, customer-state databases, event consumers, and a payment integration, with static assets and cacheable responses served from nearby content-delivery infrastructure.

The scope was deliberately narrow. Each European account had one designated write-owning region, recommendations were optional on the product page, and checkout completed without waiting for notifications, analytics, generated explanations, or assistant activity. A narrow scope let the teams define the purchase contract before they argued about resource numbers.

For the launch, a confirmed order meant that the order record was committed, the required inventory allocation was secured, and the payment authorization was recorded. Capture happened later under the fulfillment policy, so the interface never described an authorization as a completed payment. A checkout could also end with a definite rejection, or continue in a durable pending state, which meant that the application had accepted responsibility for finishing the operation and had a retrievable record and an assigned recovery path for it. Table Table summarizes the four possible outcomes.

The fourth row is the one the design aims to make impossible in normal operation. A browser can disconnect and miss a response even after the server has recorded the result. The status endpoint therefore retrieves that result by the original checkout identity, and a second submission with the same identity continues the original checkout rather than creating another order or authorization, as Chapter 3 established.

Service Objectives and Denominators

With outcomes defined, the team could say what it would measure. The three-second response interval began when the regional gateway accepted an eligible checkout request and ended when the gateway completed its response, and browser instrumentation separately measured whether the customer received and displayed that response, as Chapter 8 described. The gateway population included requests that timed out, disconnected, or never produced a normal application response, because leaving them out would improve the reported latency just when the application was failing to complete work.

The team wrote down four launch objectives before any capacity work began.

  • At least 99 percent of eligible gateway requests receive a confirmation, definite rejection, or durable pending response within three seconds.

  • At least 95 percent reach a final business outcome within three seconds, with pending responses reported separately.

  • At least 99.9 percent of accepted checkout operations have a retrievable status within 30 seconds.

  • Payment outcomes pending for more than 15 minutes trigger recovery escalation, and elapsed time alone never turns an unknown authorization into a decline.

The first two objectives measure gateway requests. The third measures distinct accepted checkout operations, so that retries cannot inflate its denominator.

A definite rejection was a timely response, but it also cost the customer a purchase. The team reviewed confirmation, rejection, and pending rates alongside the response objectives, and the product owner approved a limit of one percent for capacity-related checkout rejections over any ten-minute campaign interval. Crossing that limit required a product and capacity decision, even if the response-time objective was met. Without such a limit, a system can meet its latency target perfectly by refusing customers without doing any work.

Regional Request Path

A European request enters through the regional gateway, which authenticates the caller, attaches the checkout identity, and routes writes according to the account’s assigned owner. Figure Figure shows the layout.

Catalog reads use regional replicas under the freshness rules from Chapter 7. Cart, order, and payment writes go to their designated owner, and Inventory Service has authority over reservations and allocation. Deploying a region does not make every dependency regional or independent, so the engineers recorded the role of each required service and the checkout’s response when it is unavailable, as Table Table shows.

The line between optional and required work had a direct consequence in code. Checkout made no recommendation call at all, because even a short recommendation timeout uses up checkout time before its fallback runs. Product-page recommendations, assistant searches, and background model work each had their own admission limits, client resources, and deadlines, so that a surge of optional activity could not use the resources reserved for order processing.

Multi-Step Workflow State

A checkout calls several services, and any of those calls can be interrupted, so the design starts with a durable record. Before contacting any service that could create an external effect, Order Service created an order record for the checkout workflow, identifying the customer’s intent and the accepted cart and price snapshot. Confirmation was a later state transition on that record, not the moment the order was first saved.

On the successful path, fraud evaluation approved the accepted inputs, Inventory Service created a reservation under an identity derived from the checkout workflow, and Payment Service recorded an authorization intent before contacting the provider. After authorization, the workflow completed the inventory allocation and confirmed the order, and the confirmation transaction also inserted an outbox event for notification and analytics consumers, using the pattern from Chapter 12. If the reservation could not be converted into an allocation after authorization, the compensation rule from Chapter 3 applied. No database transaction was open during a provider call.

Partial Failure Recovery

If the sequence stops partway through, recovery uses the recorded state and operation identities. A recovery worker can continue from the interrupted step instead of starting the checkout again. Table Table lists the next permitted action at each point.

Reservation expiry needs particular care. If payment reconciliation takes longer than the inventory reservation lasts, the workflow cannot confirm the order on the strength of the earlier reservation result. It checks the current reservation state instead, and if the stock can no longer be allocated, it records a compensation operation, a void for an uncaptured authorization where the provider supports one, or a refund for a captured payment. Those compensation operations have their own identities, attempts, and pending states, and a void that has not completed does not make the financial outcome resolved. The same reasoning applies after a delayed fraud review. If the cart, price, or another material input has changed, the earlier evaluation cannot approve the revised purchase.

This state model gave the status endpoint something useful to report during an interruption, and it told recovery workers which operation to investigate.

Connection Pool Sizing

With the workflow defined, the team could estimate the resources it needed, starting with Catalog. The launch estimate put European Catalog demand at 1,440 database reads per second across the region, and the corresponding North American request class had a mean connection occupancy of 12 milliseconds. Little’s Law from Chapter 2 gives the average number of connections in use: 1,440×0.012≈17.3connections.1{,}440 \times 0.012 \approx 17.3 \quad \text{connections}.1,440×0.012≈17.3connections.

Because the estimate came from another continent’s traffic, the team also tested a planning scenario with 25 percent more reads and a mean occupancy of 18 milliseconds: 1,440×1.25×0.018=32.4connections.1{,}440 \times 1.25 \times 0.018 = 32.4 \quad \text{connections}.1,440×1.25×0.018=32.4connections.

The 18 milliseconds was a stress assumption, not a measured value. At a planning target of 70 percent utilization, that scenario called for about 46 connections across the region, which the team rounded up to 47.

The actual configuration used four Catalog instances with 20 connections each, 80 in total, and the team wrote down why the two numbers differed. Forty-seven was a pooled planning estimate. Eighty was the sum of four local limits chosen to tolerate the loss of an instance and uneven routing, because a free connection on one instance cannot serve a request waiting in another instance’s pool. With one instance down, the other three provide 60 connections, so the load test included three-instance operation, uneven routing, and the expected query mix. The database team, in turn, tested the complete connection budget across all services, including maintenance and the extra instances that run during deployments.

Capacity Claim Scope

Each sizing record stated the request class, resource, measurement interval, and deployment scope it applied to. Without that scope, a regional average can hide an instance with no spare connections, a successful four-instance test can be mistaken for evidence about three-instance operation, and a stress input can later be quoted as if it were an observed production value. Where an estimate was uncertain, the record also named the measurement that would replace it after launch. That discipline mattered most for Payment Service, where the provider imposed an external limit that no amount of application scaling could raise.

Provider Capacity and Recovery Reserves

An external provider often imposes a fleet-wide limit. Payment processors, SMS gateways, mapping APIs, and model providers like the one in Chapter 13 all do. At Baodium, the payment provider allocated European payment work a ceiling of 220 concurrent calls. That ceiling covered every operation submitted through the allocation, including calls made from another region during a failover. Baodium chose a lower operating ceiling of 200, and it did not plan to spend all of it on new authorizations, because recovery work needs provider access too.

The planning rate was 480 initial authorization attempts per second. For a stress exercise with no retry limit, the team assumed that a campaign raised initial attempts by 25 percent and that retries added another 15 percent on top. With a mean provider time of 200 milliseconds, that gives 480×1.15×1.25×0.200=138concurrent authorization calls.480 \times 1.15 \times 1.25 \times 0.200 = 138 \quad \text{concurrent authorization calls}.480×1.15×1.25×0.200=138concurrent authorization calls.

That figure deliberately ignores Baodium’s production retry budget. At the campaign rate of 600 initial calls per second, the enforced budget of 100 automatic authorization retries per minute would permit only about 1.67 extra calls per second, so offered demand at the assumed mean duration would be about (600+100/60)×0.200=120.3(600 + 100/60)\times 0.200 = 120.3(600+100/60)×0.200=120.3 concurrent calls. Neither figure includes provider calls that are still running after the local client times out. Those attempts use capacity until the provider confirms completion or its documented execution limit has passed.

Both figures cover authorization work only. Captures, voids, refunds, and status lookups use the same allocation, and some of them become more frequent just when authorizations slow down or their responses are lost. Think of a motorway during a traffic jam, where one lane is reserved for ambulances. If the jam fills every lane, the vehicles that could clear it cannot get through. The team divided the operating ceiling into classes, as Table Table shows, so that recovery work always had a lane of its own.

The normal authorization threshold of 140 leaves only two calls above the 138-call stress estimate. Under the enforced retry budget, offered demand of about 120.3 calls leaves roughly 19.7 calls of margin below normal admission. The team retained the harsher estimate as a failure rehearsal and never described the full 200-call allocation as available to new authorizations. The hard cap of 155 allows an approved increase while protecting against configuration mistakes, and new authorizations cannot borrow from the other classes.

The recovery classes needed their own tests. Fifteen concurrent status calls are not enough if lookups are slow and unresolved operations arrive faster than they can be investigated. The payment owner therefore measured the arrival rate of unresolved operations, the lookup completion rate, the age of the oldest unresolved operation, and the number of repeated lookups per operation.

Shared Admission Control

Enforcing a ceiling of 200 across several processes requires shared admission control. As Chapter 9 established for the search cluster, local limits alone cannot enforce a fleet-wide allocation. Four processes with local limits of 50 add up to 200, but a fifth process during a deployment raises the maximum to 250. Baodium routed every provider call through a shared admission and egress service, and payment instances had no provider credentials or network route of their own. Local limits were a backstop that protected each process’s own resources.

The admission service maintained durable attempt records. Before dispatching a call, it atomically checked the total and per-class allocations and recorded the accepted attempt, so a repeated submission of the same attempt identifier could not use a second allocation. Those records had to survive a failover of the admission service itself, because a replacement that lost them while provider calls continued would admit too much work. An atomic update on one server protects nothing once a failover replaces that server. Redis, for example, replicates asynchronously and can lose acknowledged writes when a replica is promoted. Recovering the admission service required durable records, fencing of the previous dispatch path, and conservative treatment of unresolved attempts. If those conditions could not be established, new dispatch stopped.

Attempt Accounting

The allocation cannot be released merely because the caller timed out. As Chapter 4 explained, the provider may still be processing the call. The admission record distinguished a completed attempt from one whose remote execution was uncertain, and an uncertain attempt retained its allocation until provider evidence showed that it had finished, or until a documented provider execution limit made that conclusion safe. An arbitrary lease expiry could not provide that evidence, and neither could a finally block that released a local permit after a network timeout.

This conservative accounting can reduce authorization capacity during a provider outage. The reserved recovery allocation lets investigation continue, but it cannot replace cooperation from the provider. If the provider offers neither a reliable completion limit nor status evidence, the team cannot promise both prompt recovery of admission capacity and a strict cap on remote execution. The team documented the limitation in the provider integration contract and required a recovery rehearsal before approving the launch.

Retry Budgets and Rejection

Retries are the other source of extra provider load. At a 30 percent retry rate, 480 first attempts per second create another 144 calls per second, which is the kind of surge that arrives during a degraded interval. Production allowed at most 100 automatic authorization retries per minute across the whole allocation, using the retry budget from Chapter 9, and each retry also needed ordinary class admission. Gateway, service-mesh, and provider-client retries were configured so that one designated component owned the retry decision, and a browser resubmission retrieved or continued the existing checkout identity.

A new attempt rejected by admission received a retry-later response before any provider call, but only when the workflow had established that no earlier authorization for the same intent was unresolved. If an earlier attempt was uncertain, the customer received the pending status instead.

Decision review

How would you spend the provider allowance?

The European payment allocation is a ceiling of 220 concurrent calls. Four Payment Service processes run in steady state, and deployments briefly run a fifth. Authorizations at peak need about 140 concurrent calls. Captures, status lookups, and reconciliation share the remainder. Someone proposes a local limit of 50 calls per process, which looks conservative against 220.

Set the local limit to 50 per process. Four processes give 200, comfortably inside 220.

Set the local limit to 44, so five processes fit within 220 during a deployment.

Use local limits as a backstop and enforce the 220 centrally.

A fails during a deployment. Five processes at 50 permit 250 concurrent calls against an allowance of 220, and the fifth process appears during a deployment, when other changes are usually under way as well.

B fixes the arithmetic but wastes capacity. In steady state, four processes at 44 can use only 176 of the 220 calls, leaving 44 unused, and the limit has to be recalculated whenever the fleet is resized.

C uses shared admission, as Section Section describes. It adds a dependency that needs its own availability target and a defined response when it is unreachable. Local limits are a backstop, but five local limits of 50 permit 250 calls if central admission fails open, so respecting the provider ceiling also means refusing new calls when admission is unavailable and accounting for remote work already dispatched.

Whichever option you choose, reserve capacity for the recovery classes before distributing the rest. Status lookups resolve uncertain authorizations and captures complete authorized payments, and both need an allocation when new authorizations have used up their own.

Deadline Propagation and Dependency Budgets

Capacity limits decide how much processing runs concurrently, and deadlines decide how long each piece may take. The gateway assigned one deadline to each checkout request, and required services received the time left under that deadline and applied their own caps within it, as Chapter 4 described. Figure Figure shows the allocation.

The three seconds covered validation, risk evaluation, inventory reservation, authorization, local persistence, and the response path, and no dependency received a fresh three seconds of its own. For launch testing, the team started from the allocations in Table Table.

These are upper limits, and most calls finish well inside them. Before starting authorization, Payment Service reserved time for handling the result locally, and the provider call received the smaller of its two-second cap and the time left. That figure was recalculated after admission and connection acquisition, because waiting for either uses part of the allowance. If preparation could not finish in time, the application returned a rejection or a durable pending state before starting payment. If authorization had already been submitted, deadline expiry preserved the uncertain operation for recovery.

Circuit breakers limited later calls once failures and slow completions had been observed, but they work alongside concurrency admission rather than replacing it, as Chapter 9 showed. In the first seconds of a slowdown, active calls can fill the allocation before the breaker has seen enough completed calls to open.

Regional Write Ownership

The design review returned to its original concern. Which region may accept a payment? Routing chooses a destination, but ownership decides which region may accept writes for a customer at a given moment. The mechanism is the shard directory from Chapter 7, applied at the scale of a region.

Think of a relay race. At any moment, a single runner carries the baton, and a handover is a short, deliberate exchange, not two runners each producing a baton of their own. An account’s write-owning region was assigned independently of where the customer happened to be. A European customer visiting New York could use nearby static content and read replicas, but account, cart, order, and payment writes went to the assigned European owner. The design accepted some extra network time in exchange for a single, defined place to write.

An ownership record contained the account or ownership group, its region, its state, and an epoch that increases with every reassignment. Routing caches used the record to choose a destination, and the receiving service checked the active owner and epoch before changing local state. A stale routing cache could cause a rejected command, but it could never grant a region write authority it did not have.

The ownership records themselves lived in a consensus-backed control service, built on a system such as etcd or ZooKeeper, whose quorum spanned separate failure domains. Two application regions on their own cannot form a control plane that survives the loss of either one, because neither side can tell whether the other has failed or is merely unreachable, so teams usually add a small third location that acts only as a tiebreaker. When quorum was unavailable, ownership transfers stopped, and existing owners continued only under the documented authorization policy.

Planned Ownership Transfer

Changing the ownership record is only one step of a transfer, because a record cannot revoke an old database session or cancel a provider request that has already been sent. The transfer procedure closes the old write and dispatch paths before activating the new owner, using the same idea as the shard transfer in Chapter 7.

  1. The control service marks the ownership group as transferring and stops new work for it.

  2. The previous owner stops accepting writes, completes or terminates existing transactions, and prevents stale workers from resuming.

  3. The provider egress path stops dispatching new attempts for the old assignment, and attempts already sent are completed or recorded as unresolved.

  4. Engineers establish the final replication position and verify that the destination has the required workflow, idempotency, and outbox records.

  5. The destination installs the next epoch, and the control service activates the new owner.

  6. Verification confirms that old-owner commands are rejected and that the new owner can retrieve the status of existing operations.

Fencing has to match the scope of the transfer, because revoking a region-wide credential to transfer one account interrupts unrelated accounts. A stale database epoch is good evidence for rejecting a database command, but the payment provider has no way to check database epochs, so provider dispatch needs its own enforcement at the egress service. If any required fence cannot be established, the destination does not open writes.

Unplanned Failover and Data Loss

An unplanned regional failure takes away the chance to inspect the old primary and read its final replication position. An asynchronous replica may be missing a checkout intent, a completed authorization record, or an outbox entry, and promoting it without examining the gap could permit a new authorization while the provider has already completed the original.

The launch policy distinguished restoring service from recovering all state. For payment and order records, the team did not claim lossless failover from an asynchronous replica. It required either evidence that the destination had the necessary acknowledged operations, or a procedure that reconstructed and reconciled the gap, and new affected writes were suspended during that work. Zero loss of acknowledged records after a full regional failure requires durable acknowledgment from an independent failure domain before reporting acceptance, which adds latency and can reduce write availability when the regions cannot reach each other.

Two recovery objectives define these trade-offs. The recovery-time objective states how soon service should resume, and the recovery-point objective states how much committed data may be lost. If a shop’s power fails, the first is how long until the doors reopen, and the second is how many of the last receipts may be missing from the books. Both were documented per kind of data and tested, not assumed from the existence of a replica. Backups provided a separate path for deletion or corruption, which replication faithfully copies to the standby, and restore exercises included the operation records needed to reconcile external effects.

Cross-Region Operation Identity

A payment’s identity has to survive routing and ownership changes. The provider idempotency key combined the operation type with a unique operation identifier, while region and epoch were recorded only as execution metadata. An authorization, a capture, a void, and a refund are separate intents with separate identities, and a regional retry of one authorization reuses that authorization’s original identity.

The provider’s idempotency scope needed the same scrutiny. If Europe and North America used separate merchant accounts, the same key might not identify one operation across both. Failover therefore reused the provider account and contract needed to retrieve or retry the original operation, and an uncertain authorization was never sent to another provider as though no earlier attempt existed. Provider retention periods were part of the recovery policy too, because once an idempotency record may have expired, resubmitting the key no longer guarantees that a second effect is suppressed, as Chapter 3 warned.

Asynchronous Work and Recovery Throughput

The order confirmation and its outbox event commit in one local transaction, and everything downstream obeys the rules from Chapter 12. The relay may publish an event more than once, consumers deduplicate, and each consumer has its own completion point. The launch dashboard showed the oldest unpublished outbox event, consumer progress, the oldest unfinished notification task, provider acceptance, and failed or quarantined work.

Recovery tests ran while new events were still arriving. Clearing 40,000 queued events in 20 minutes requires about 33 completions per second above the ongoing arrival rate, assuming comparable work per event: 40,00020×60≈33.3additional completions per second.\frac{40{,}000}{20 \times 60} \approx 33.3 \quad \text{additional completions per second}.20×6040,000​≈33.3additional completions per second.

A test that stops producers never measures that margin, and a test that watches only broker lag can miss email tasks piling up further downstream. Replay obeyed each consumer’s correctness rules. An analytical projection could be rebuilt into an isolated destination, while replaying notifications required protection against resending.

European Launch Release Gates

The launch combined a new region with new configuration, so the release team took care not to treat every difference from North America as a software regression. Pre-launch tests exercised the European infrastructure, and once a European baseline existed, application canaries were compared with stable instances in the same region, while the absolute service objectives applied throughout. Canary routing preserved representative per-instance load, for the reason Chapter 10 explained.

The first stage used five percent exposure, and each promotion decision required two nonoverlapping five-minute windows with at least 2,000 eligible canary requests each. Every criterion was written so that a reviewer could mark it met or not met from recorded evidence, as Table Table shows.

Version-specific comparisons and regional totals were both needed, because shared dependencies affect stable and canary instances together. A canary that adds database work can slow stable requests as well, so a small gap between the two groups gives little reassurance on its own.

Removing candidate exposure changes future routing only. Requests already sent, committed rows, emitted events, and provider effects take their normal completion or recovery paths, so application rollback was tested against rows and events the candidate had created, and schema and message compatibility used the procedure from Chapter 10. A rollback restores earlier code. It cannot undo a completed authorization or an incompatible data change.

Failure Rehearsal Before Launch

Two weeks before launch, the responders scheduled for production duty ran the runbooks themselves, using their production-equivalent access. Many teams call this a game day. A rehearsal like this tests more than whether components restart. It exposes missing permissions, outdated commands, and steps that need access the responders do not have, while there is still time to fix them. A runbook the on-call team has never used under pressure is still a hypothesis.

The rehearsals interrupted the payment provider, regional routing, and event consumers while requests were in progress. One interrupted checkout after the provider accepted an authorization but before Payment Service recorded the result. Another expired an inventory reservation during reconciliation, and a third interrupted the admission service while provider attempts were active. The regional exercise delayed replication and made the previous owner unreachable, so that responders had to establish whether the destination could accept writes and identify the evidence that was missing. The event exercise introduced 40,000 queued records, including duplicates and malformed messages, while new events were still arriving. Table Table lists the result each scenario had to produce.

The runbook also defined what to do when a rehearsal failed. If responders could not prove that the old provider path had been disabled, payment writes did not reopen in the destination, and the outcome was recorded as a recovery limitation to resolve, not as a successful failover on the grounds that the new application instances were ready.

Post-Launch Measurements and Revisions

Production then supplied the European measurements the launch estimates had lacked, and the team sized each difference before changing any plan.

Catalog demand reached 1,692 reads per second, about 18 percent above the planned 1,440, and mean connection occupancy in the same interval was 13 milliseconds: 1,692×0.013≈22.0connections.1{,}692 \times 0.013 \approx 22.0 \quad \text{connections}.1,692×0.013≈22.0connections.

A separate short-window peak reached 54 assigned connections across the four instances. The team did not compare that peak with the average estimate, because the two measure different things. Instead, the engineers inspected per-instance assignments, acquisition time, and request mix, because 54 of 80 regional connections says nothing about whether any one local pool ran out. The measurements revised the forecast, the reduced-instance test was repeated, and the 80-connection configuration was retained only because those results supported it.

A later recommendation configuration change caused one request class to fetch candidate products in a loop. In the canary group, database queries per lookup for that class rose from 1.0 to 1.6. Each query was as fast as before, so mean occupancy barely changed and the latency alert did not fire. The increase appeared in the query rate, the other half of the product from Chapter 1, which an occupancy gate alone could never catch. The queries-per-request comparison failed both five-minute windows, the release controller removed the candidate, and the team fixed the configuration before trying again.

During the first campaign, provider authorization p95 reached 1,900 milliseconds, nearly ten times the 200-millisecond planning assumption. A percentile cannot give mean concurrency, however, so before revising capacity, the payment owner collected aligned measurements of offered rate, admitted rate, completion rate, mean attempt duration, outstanding attempts, and rejections. Admission records showed where new attempts had been refused, and those refusals were reviewed against the one percent rejection limit, because prompt retry-later responses are not evidence that customers could buy what they wanted.

Four authorizations entered reconciliation after their responses were lost. Recovery retrieved the provider results under the original identities and checked inventory and order state before completing each workflow. Notification processing also built up a campaign backlog, but the orders had already committed, so customers could see them while the notification workers caught up, and the notification owner measured the delay through provider acceptance rather than consumer progress.

The team revised the admission and recovery budgets using those measurements. Catalog sizing switched to European observations, payment planning required campaign measurements and a review of the provider allocation, and the release criteria retained the queries-per-request comparison that had caught the recommendation regression.

Five-Question Design Review

The European launch needed more detail than most applications do. A new service with one database and a modest workload may have no reason for regional ownership transfers or a shared provider-admission service, but it still has decisions to make about accepted work, resource limits, failure responses, and recovery. For a new checkout, booking flow, file upload, or background job, we can use five questions to organize the design review.

  1. What has the application promised? Identify the accepted operation, the response deadline, and the evidence required to report success, including pending and rejected outcomes.

  2. Which work can one request create? Account for dependency calls, retries, fan-out, generated work, and asynchronous tasks, and assign each one to a resource allocation.

  3. What survives interruption? Identify the durable operation, its current owner, its state transitions, and the external effects that recovery must investigate.

  4. What happens when a limit is reached? Decide which requests are refused, which work can be deferred, and which resources are reserved for recovery.

  5. Which evidence changes the decision? Specify the measurement, its denominator and interval, the resulting action, and the response when the evidence is unavailable.

We already worked through those decisions in the earlier chapters. For this launch, the team wrote down the payment-state guarantee, the estimated provider limit, the conditions for transferring regional ownership, and the evidence required before increasing exposure. A smaller application might need only a page of review notes. The record should still say who owns each decision and what evidence would justify revising it, because the people operating the next release may not have attended the original design review.

Regional Authority and Recovery Revision

Returning to the first drawing shows how much the review changed. The proposal in Figure Figure placed regional application stacks and customer databases behind a traffic router. Each stack had a payment client and a local pool of worker capacity. Under normal conditions, the proposal appeared to offer low latency and a second region for failover. The review then found several unsupported assumptions about write ownership, payment state, and recovery capacity.

The first problem in the review concerned write ownership. If both regions accepted updates for a European account during a network partition, asynchronous replication could create competing order states. If one region failed after acknowledging an authorization but before replicating its record, the second region could lack the operation identity needed to investigate a retry. The team assigned one write authority for each account, required durable operation identities before dispatch, and defined an ownership-transfer procedure that fences the former writer. A replica could be promoted only after the recovery requirements for its missing writes were understood.

The second problem concerned capacity. Redirecting traffic to a backup region increased load on application instances, database pools, and the shared payment provider at the same time. Each allocation needed a degraded-region estimate. The provider budget also needed capacity for reconciliation, so a recovery mechanism that competed with new authorizations could not consume the entire allowance. The allocations calculated earlier in the chapter are this revised capacity plan, because adding a second region alone would not reserve capacity for recovery.

The third problem concerned customer outcomes. A payment timeout could occur after the provider authorized a transaction. The initial proposal had only success and failure responses, leaving no durable place for an uncertain result. The revised workflow records the operation identity and pending state, retrieves provider evidence under that identity, and confirms an order only after its required inventory and authorization facts are established. Notification and analytics workers do not affect the checkout confirmation path.

The launch rehearsal then challenged each revision. The team simulated loss of a region during a pending authorization, a provider slowdown during retry traffic, and a lagging replica during ownership transfer. A successful test required matching operation records and provider outcomes, verified fencing, and sufficient capacity for customer traffic and recovery. A request that was rejected promptly could protect provider capacity while still violating a customer acceptance objective. The release decision examined resource utilization alongside the successful completion and refusal rates customers experienced.

The review rejected the first proposal before the first European payment. The revised design names its authority, records enough state to recover, allocates scarce capacity, and identifies the evidence that would invalidate its assumptions. You can run this review for a new SaaS control plane, a cross-region document service, or a messaging platform changing its write owners.

Summary

The launch review began with one question about a failure at 14:05 and ended with a different architecture. That is what designing from production experience means for a team. The first drawing was reasonable. It became safe only after the team asked, for every important operation, who is allowed to decide, what record survives an interruption, which resource is scarce, and what evidence would show the plan was wrong.

You have now seen each of those questions on its own. Capacity estimates from Chapters 1 and 2, operation identity from Chapter 3, deadlines and admission from Chapters 4 and 9, data authority from Chapters 7 and 11, release gates from Chapter 10, and recovery from Chapter 12. The difficulty in an actual launch is that they all arrive together, and fixing one can break another. Writing assumptions down, attaching a measurement and an owner to each, and rehearsing the failures before customers depend on them is how a team manages that complexity.

You can apply the same review to a new SaaS region, a banking service, or a messaging platform. Appendix B does that for four systems that look nothing like Baodium, and it is a good place to practice the habits from this book on problems you have not seen before.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & European planning uses North American measurements. Catalog has four pools of 20 connections, and Payment has a 200-call operating ceiling that includes protected recovery capacity.
Condition that tests it & Provider durations exceed the planning distribution, demand exceeds the forecast, or checkout ownership must transfer between regions.
Constraint or invariant & Orders are confirmed only with authorization, inventory allocation, and committed state. The former write and dispatch paths are fenced before a new region accepts writes.
Evidence and uncertainty & Modeled authorization concurrency is 138 in the unconstrained stress case and about 120 under the retry budget, against normal admission at 140 and a class cap of 155.

Still unknown: how long remote work outlasts local timeouts during a provider slowdown, and which acknowledged writes an asynchronous replica would lack after an unplanned regional failure.
Signal and evaluation window & Regional occupancy and customer outcomes, compared at each exposure step and throughout reduced-capacity and failover tests.
Control and decision & Revise allocations from European measurements, pause expansion when objectives or correctness checks fail, and preserve operation identities and recovery records.
Owner and review trigger & Payment owns unresolved operations. Inventory owns reservations. Release Engineering controls exposure. SRE coordinates recovery. Review before campaign expansion or a regional transfer.
